abstract.p: Inspired by light-front holography, we compute the pion mass, charge radius, decay constant, electromagnetic form factor and electromagnetic transition form factor. To do so, we model the longitudinal quark dynamics using potentials due to ’t Hooft and to Li and Vary. We find a longitudinal wave function that is rather more peaked about x∼1/2 than in previous studies. We also explore the strong degeneracy between these two potentials and conclude by noting that one scenario that accords well with the data also maps onto an equation previously noted by Vegh that describes the dynamics of a four-segmented string in three-dimensional anti–de Sitter spacetime.

sec.label: I.
sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p:
The pion occupies a special status in particle physics. In the quark model, it is a quark-antiquark meson and yet it is much lighter than all other mesons. In QCD, it is simultaneously a bound state of quarks and gluons and a pseudo-Goldstone boson of chiral symmetry breaking. Its physical properties thus offer a unique window into the intertwined phenomena of confinement and chiral symmetry breaking [1]. This elusive physics is encoded in the Gell-Mann–Oakes–Renner (GMOR) relation [2], fπ2Mπ2=2mq|⟨q¯q⟩|+O(mq2),(1)where Mπ is the pion mass, fπ its decay constant, mq is the light-quark mass1
We assume isospin symmetry. and ⟨q¯q⟩ is the quark condensate. Equation (1) is supported by lattice calculations [3] and predicts that, in the chiral limit, the pion mass vanishes as Mπ2∝mq while fπ remains finite.

Light-front holography (LFH) (for a review, see [4]) is a realization of Maldacena’s AdS/CFT correspondence [5] in the conformal limit of QCD where quark masses and quantum loops are ignored. Light-front holography predicts that the pion is massless. To generate the physical pion mass, nonzero quark masses need to be taken into account. As a first approximation, this can be achieved using a prescription by Brodsky and de Téramond [6] known as the invariant mass ansatz (IMA) which is widely used in the phenomenology of light mesons [4]. In a previous Letter [7], we used the IMA with the light-front holographic wave function to successfully predict diffractive ρ electroproduction. However, the IMA predicts that [8] Mπ2≈2mq2ln(κ2/mq2-γE), where γE is the Euler constant, instead of Eq. (1). For this reason, the IMA becomes questionable, at least for the pion.

Recently, there have been attempts to go beyond the IMA by modeling the longitudinal dynamics in mesons [8–12] using the ’t Hooft (tH) [13] and Li-Vary (LV) [14] equations2
Alternative models for longitudinal dynamics are reviewed in [15]. For longitudinal dynamics with chiral perturbation theory constraints or in a graviton soft-wall model, see [16] or [17]. so that Eq. (1) is satisfied. Each of these papers has a different focus with the parameters of a given model varying significantly between the papers. With the exception of Ref. [10], none of these papers consider simultaneously the three precisely measured, nonperturbative pion observables3
Mπ=139.57039±1.8×10-4 MeV, fπ=130.2±1.7 MeV, rπ=0.659±0.004 fm [18].: Mπ, fπ and the charge radius rπ. Reference [10] does so, together with form factor data, but overestimates fπ.

Among light mesons, the pion is most sensitive to longitudinal dynamics since, as we shall see, its mass is entirely generated by it. Our goal in this paper is to focus exclusively on the nonperturbative behavior of the pion and in so doing we are able to explore the well-established degeneracy between the ground-states of the tH and LV models [9,11,13]. We fix the model parameters using the mass, decay constant and charge radius and then compare to the form factor data, where we find very good agreement in the low Q2 region. We also point out that an equation due to Vegh [19], obtained by studying the dynamics of a segmented string in three-dimensional anti–de Sitter spacetime (AdS3), coincides with a viable scenario.

sec.label: II.
sec.title: TRANSVERSE AND LONGITUDINAL DYNAMICS
sec.p: Our starting point is light-front QCD, where the Schrödinger-like equation for mesons reads [20] (-∇2x(1-x)+mq2x+mq¯21-x+U(x,b))Ψ(x,b)=M2Ψ(x,b),(2)where M is the meson mass and Ψ(x,b) is the meson’s wave function, with x being the light-front momentum fraction carried by the quark and b=(b⊥,φ) the transverse displacement of the quark and antiquark. Assuming isospin symmetry, we take mu=md≡mq. The confining potential U cannot yet be derived from first principles in QCD although, as we shall see, progress has been achieved using light-front holography and its extensions. The normalization condition on the wave function is ∫d2bdx|Ψ(x,b)|2=1,(3)which embodies the assumption that the pion consists only of the leading qq¯ Fock sector.

We introduce the transverse vector ζ=x(1-x)b such that, under the assumption [21], U(x,b)=U⊥(ζ)+U∥(x),(4)Equation (2) can be solved by a separation of variables, i.e. Ψ(x,b)=ϕ(ζ)2πζeiLφX(x),(5)where L is the relative orbital angular momentum of the qq¯ pair. Equation (2) separates into [-d2dζ2+4L2-14ζ2+U⊥]ϕ(ζ)=M⊥2ϕ(ζ)(6)and [mq2x(1-x)+U∥]X(x)=M∥2X(x)(7)with M2=M⊥2+M∥2. Choosing ∫0∞dζ|ϕ(ζ)|2=1,(8)Equation (3) implies that ∫01dxx(1-x)|X(x)|2=1.(9)It is useful to define χ(x)=X(x)/x(1-x), so that Eq. (7) becomes [mq2x(1-x)+V∥]χ(x)=M∥2χ(x),(10)where V∥=1x(1-x)U∥x(1-x)(11)and ∫01dx|χ(x)|2=1.(12)Interestingly, Eq. (10) coincides with the tH equation for mesons in (1+1)-dimensional, large-Nc QCD; suggesting that V∥ may be the ’t Hooft potential operator [13]. This is the choice made in Refs. [10,12]. On the other hand, Ref. [21], which was the first paper to extend light-front holography by accounting for longitudinal dynamics, chooses U∥ to be the tH potential operator. Alternatively, Refs. [8,9] choose V∥ to be the LV potential operator [14].

More generally, the eigenspectrum of Eq. (10) is invariant under the similarity transformation V∥→h(x)V∥1h(x)(13)for some h(x), while the eigenfunctions transform as χ(x)→h(x)χ(x).(14)As we will motivate later, we consider h(x)=[x(1-x)]n/2 and take V∥ to be the tH or LV operator as our default (i.e. n=0). In this language, Ref. [21] takes n=-1 while Refs. [8–11] choose n=0. It turns out that n<0 is badly behaved in the chiral limit (see Appendix B). We will also see that the pion data exclude n≥3 while the remaining possibilities, n=0,1,2, are all able to fit the data. We refer to the n=0,1,2 cases as models A, B, C respectively. For example, model tH-B means that V∥ is the ’t Hooft potential operator with n=1.

Equation (6) is the holographic Schrödinger equation, derived by de Téramond and Brodsky [22], where the variable ζ maps onto the fifth dimension in AdS5, with [4] U⊥=ULFH=κ4ζ2+2κ2(J-1),(15)where J is the spin of the meson and κ is an emerging confinement scale. It is argued in [23] that the analytic form of U⊥, given by Eq. (15), is uniquely fixed by the underlying conformal symmetry and holographic mapping to AdS5. The mass scale κ in the harmonic (first) term of Eq. (15) does not spoil the conformal symmetry of the underlying action. Then, the holographic mapping implies that a quadratic dilaton deforms the geometry of pure AdS5 (this is referred to as the soft-wall model [24]) and this fixes the constant (second) term in Eq. (15).

Solving Eq. (6) using Eq. (15) yields M⊥2(n⊥,J,L)=4κ2(n⊥+J+L2),(16)which predicts that the lowest-lying meson, with n⊥=J=L=0, is massless. It is natural to identify this state with the pion. The corresponding wave function is [4] ϕπ(ζ)=κ2ζexp(-κ2ζ22).(17)Using Eq. (5), the pion wave function is thus Ψπ(x,b)=κπx(1-x)χ(x)exp(-κ2x(1-x)b⊥22),(18)where χ(x) is now the lowest eigenfunction of Eq. (10).

Armed with Eq. (18) and a form for V∥, we are able to compute a number of important properties of the pion. Specifically, we focus on the pion mass (Mπ), decay constant (fπ), electromagnetic form factor [Fπ(Q2)] and the pion-to-photon transition form factor [Fπγ(Q2)]. The pion mass is given by Eq. (10), Mπ2=∫01dxχ*(x)[mq2x(1-x)+V∥]χ(x)(19)and the other quantities can be computed using (e.g. see [12,25]) fπ=6π∫01dxΨπ(x,0)=6πκ∫01dxx(1-x)χ(x),(20)Fπ(Q2)=π∫01dxdb⊥2J0((1-x)b⊥Q)|Ψπ(x,b)|2=∫01dx|χ(x)|2exp(-(1-x)xQ24κ2)(21)and Q2Fπγ(Q2)=2κ3π∫01dxx(1-x)χ(x)×∫0∞db⊥(mqb⊥)K1(mqb⊥)⁢exp(-κ2x(1-x)b⊥22)QJ1(b⊥(1-x)Q),(22)which is derived in Appendix A.

There are two further quantities of interest. The pion charge radius, which is related to the Q2→0 limit of the form factor (FF), rπ2=-6limQ2→0dFπ(Q2)dQ2=32κ2∫01dx(1-x)x|χ(x)|2,(23)and the π0→γγ decay width, which is related to the Q2→0 limit of the transition form factor (TFF), Γγγ=π4αem2Mπ3|Fπγ(0)|2.(24)Our attention must now turn to the form of the longitudinal potential V∥ and its lowest-lying eigenfunction.

sec.label: III.
sec.title: THE LI-VARY MODEL
sec.p: A model for V∥ that admits an exact power-law solution for its ground state is the phenomenological QCD potential first proposed by Li et al. [14] and further studied by Li and Vary [8]. The LV potential operator is V∥LV=-σ2∂x(x(1-x)∂x)(25)and the lowest-lying eigenfunction is [8,9] χ(x)=N(β)xβ(1-x)β(26)with β=mq/σ. We see that χ(x)→1 in the chiral limit (mq→0), which is the same form as that predicted using holography in [26–28]. The various observables are then given by Mπ=σ2β(1+2β),(27)fπ=N(β)κ6π122(1+β)Γ(3/2+β)Γ(2+4β),(28)rπ2=3(1+2β)4κ2β,(29)Fπ(Q2)=N(β)2Γ(1+2β)U(1+2β,-2β,Q24κ2),(30)where U is the confluent hypergeometric function of the second kind and N(β)2=Γ(2+4β)Γ(1+2β).(31)

For the potentials given by Eq. (13), all observables except for Eq. (27) can still be computed using the above equations with n successive replacements β→β+1/2. The pion mass is the exception since it is invariant under the similarity transformations [recall that Mπ2=M∥2, i.e. it is the eigenvalue of Eq. (10)]. Note that Eq. (27) implies that Mπ2=2σmq+4mq2,(32)i.e. the LV models are consistent with the GMOR relation.

Since the decay constant and radius depend only upon κ and β we use their measured values to fix these two parameters. The remaining parameter σ can then be determined from the pion mass. In Table I we show the resulting values of κ, mq and σ for the LV-A, LV-B and LV-C models. Notice that the preferred values of β=mq/σ are very close to 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5. This means that X(x)∝[x(1-x)]2, which is considerably more peaked than the X(x)∝x(1-x) form anticipated in [26–28].

caption.p: Extracted values of the parameters of the LV model discussed in the text.

sec.p: We are now in a position to postdict the form factor data and in Fig. 1 we show the results for the LV models. Agreement with the data is excellent for low values of Q2, which accords with the fact that we do not include any perturbative QCD evolution. All three forms of the LV potential give identical results for the FF, since it depends only upon κ and β. The TFF has some very weak dependence on mq.

caption.p: Postdictions of the LV models for the FF data [29–36] and TFF data [37–40].

sec.p: The decay width that we obtain using the Q2→0 limit of Eq. (22) is Γγγ=7.0, 7.2, 7.4 eV for LV-A, LV-B, LV-C. This compares favorably to the experimental measurement of 7.82±0.22 eV [18], though we do note that Eq. (22) is missing nonperturbative corrections to the photon wave function as Q2→0. Better agreement with experiment is obtained if we use the Adler-Bell-Jackiw (ABJ) chiral anomaly relation, Fπγ(0)=122π2fπ,(33)in Eq. (24), in which case all three models necessarily give Γγγ=7.8 eV. This is simply the statement that the data are in accord with the ABJ relation.

sec.label: IV.
sec.title: THE ’T HOOFT MODEL
sec.p: Another candidate for V∥ is the ’t Hooft model, in which case Eq. (10) becomes [13] mq2-g2x(1-x)χ(x)-g2P∫01dyχ(y)(x-y)2=M∥2χ(x),(34)where the principal value prescription is defined as P∫dyf(x,y)(x-y)2≡limε→0+12∫dy(f(x,y)(x-y+iε)2+f(x,y)(x-y-iε)2).(35)No analytical solution to Eq. (34) is known and it has to be solved numerically. However, it is known that χ(x)∼xβ or χ(x)∼(1-x)β at the end points, x→0, 1, as a consequence of the Hamiltonian being Hermitian [13,41]. In fact, as illustrated in Fig. 5, χ(x)∼[x(1-x)]β is a very good approximation for the ground state wave function in the tH model across the entire range in x. The end point analysis of Eq. (34) yields [13,21] mq2-g2+g2πβcot(πβ)=0,(36)where we have used [41] -P∫01dyχ(y)(x-y)2→-P∫0∞dyyβ(x-y)2=πβcot(πβ)xβ-1(37)if x→0. For any χ(x) that satisfies Eq. (34) [11], ∫dx(P∫01dyχ(y)(x-y)2)=0.(38)After integrating Eq. (34) using Eq. (38) we find Mπ2mq2=2β+4.(39)For β≪1, Eq. (36) implies that β=mq/(3gπ), so that Eq. (39) implies Mπ2∝mq to leading order in mq, i.e. we recover the GMOR relation. Agreement with the GMOR relation is also confirmed in [42,43]. Equation (34) therefore predicts that χ(x)→1 in the chiral limit.

Following the same methodology as in the previous section, we show the result of fixing the tH model parameters using the measured values of the charged pion mass, decay constant and radius in Table II. Our postdictions for the FF data using the tH model are shown in Fig. 2 and, not surprisingly, the results are almost identical to those in the LV model.

caption.p: Postdictions of the tH models for the FF data [29–36] and TFF data [37–40].
Extracted values of the parameters of the tH models discussed in the text.

sec.p: Using the Q2→0 limit of Eq. (22), we obtain Γγγ=7.2, 7.4, 7.6 eV for tH-A, tH-B, tH-C, which is very similar to the corresponding numbers for the LV models.

sec.label: V.
sec.title: A THIRD MODEL
sec.p: To investigate the correlation between the tH and LV models we introduce a third model, (mq2-g2x(1-x))χ(x)-g2P∫01dyχ(y)(x-y)2-σ2∂x(x(1-x)∂x)χ(x)=M∥2χ(x),(40)which we refer to as the FS-A model. If mq=g, 4gs=g2/σ2, μ2=M∥2/g2 and x=z, Eq. (40) becomes the quantum spectral curve of a four-segmented string in AdS3 derived by Vegh [19], -P∫01dz′χ(z′)(z-z′)2-14gs∂z(z(1-z)∂z)χ(z)=μ2χ(z),(41)where gs is the string tension in units of the AdS radius (squared).

If instead we choose mq2=g2+σ2/4, Eq. (40) becomes -P∫01dz′χ(z′)(z-z′)2-14gsz(1-z)∂z2(z(1-z)χ(z))=μ2χ(z),(42)where we have used the fact that ∂x(x(1-x)∂x)χ(x)=x(1-x)∂x2(x(1-x)χ(x))+14x(1-x)χ(x).(43)Equation (42) is a second possibility for the string equation in AdS3. The two possibilities arise from the two ways to symmetrize the weak-coupling term in the string Hamiltonian [19]. Notice that the constraint, mq2=g2+σ2/4, together with 4gs=g2/σ2 implies that g≤mq since gs≥0.

Figure 3 explores the correlation between the tH and LV models. The quark mass varies very weakly along each ellipse. Notice that FS-C is able to accommodate the holographic constraint, g2+σ2/4=mq2 in the σ≫g limit, which is equivalent to a weak string coupling, gs≪1. Viewed this way, one could regard our observation that mq=σ/2 in the LV-C model as a prediction of the AdS3 string equation. Though without a firmer basis for the correspondence this is speculative.

caption.p: Exploring the correlation between the tH and LV potentials via the FS models. Each point on a given curve represents a pair (g,σ) of extracted parameters using the pion data. Note that mq varies very weakly along each curve between its tH and LV limits: see Tables I and II. The solid green curve, labeled as AdS, is the holographic constraint g2+σ2/4=mq2 with mq=48.2 MeV (which lies in between its tH-C and LV-C limits).

sec.p: Finally, we should comment upon the fact that our extracted value of κ=423 MeV is much lower than the typical value, κ≈500 MeV, that fits the Regge slopes for light mesons [4]. Previous work on the pion using holography also require smaller values of κ: κ=375 MeV in [27], κ=361 MeV in [44], κ≈370 MeV in [45], and κ=432 MeV in [46].

sec.label: VI.
sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: We have used the ’t Hooft and Li-Vary potentials to model the longitudinal dynamics in the pion. For the transverse dynamics we use the well-established light-front holographic Schrödinger equation. Using only the low energy pion data to fix the parameters of the models, we find very good agreement with the low Q2 form factor data and a longitudinal momentum distribution that is considerably more peaked about x∼1/2 than in previous studies. We have also explored the degeneracy between the tH and LV models. Our analysis of the longitudinal dynamics is in accord with an equation derived by Vegh to describe the dynamics of a four-segmented string in AdS3.

app.title: DERIVATION OF THE TRANSITION FORM FACTOR
app.p:
Using the loop diagram in Fig. 4, we derive Eq. (22) for the pion-to-photon transition factor Fπγ(Q2) which is defined via [25] ⟨γ(P′)|JEMμ|π0(P)⟩=iFπγ(Q2)εμνρσPνϵρqσ(A1)where JEMμ is the quark EM current given by JEMμ=efΨ¯(0)γμΨ(0)(A2)with ef being the electric charge, in units of e, of the quark (flavor f) and (Ψ¯)Ψ are the (adjoint) quark-field operators evaluated at the same spacetime point. The 4-momentum of the virtual photon is qσ=Pσ′-Pσ, with q2≡-Q2, while εμνρσ is the Levi-Civita totally antisymmetric tensor and ϵρ is polarization 4-vector of the transversely polarized real photon. In the q+=0 frame, Pμ=(P+,Mπ2+Q2P+,q),(A3)and qμ=(0,-Mπ2+Q2P+,-q)(A4)so that Q2=q⊥2 where q⊥=|q|. For the polarization vector of the real photon, we choose ϵρ=12(0,0,1,i).(A5)Taking μ=+ in Eq. (A1), and using Eqs. (A3)–(A5), yields ⟨γ(P′)|JEM+|π0(P)⟩=12Fπγ(Q2)P+Q.(A6)The Fock expansion of the matrix element on the left-hand side is ⟨γ(P′)|JEMμ|π0(P)⟩=ef4πNc∑h,ℏ∫dxd2k16π3Ψh,h¯*γ⁢(x,k-(1-x)q)Ψh,h¯π(x,k)×{v¯h¯(1-x,-k)x(1-x)γμuh(x,k)x},(A7)where h(h¯)=± are the quark (antiquark) helicities. The factor Nc originates from the product of two color factors: Nc from the sum over all colors in the quark loop and 1/Nc from the color singlet wave function for the pion. The factor 4π accounts for a mismatch of convention between the normalization of the meson wave function used in this paper and that used in the light-front formalism. Specifically, we use [47] ∑h,h¯∫d2k4π2dx|Ψh,h¯(x,k)|2=1,(A8)which is consistent with Eq. (3), whereas the light-front formalism uses [48] ∑h,h¯∫d2k16π3dx|Ψh,h¯(x,k)|2=1.(A9)In Eq. (A7), Ψh,-ℏ*γ(x,k-(1-x)q) is the real photon light-front wave function (complex conjugated) and Ψh,ℏπ(x,k) is the pion light-front wave function. Now, taking μ=+ in Eq. (A7), we find ⟨γ(P′)|JEM+|π0(P)⟩=2P+ef4πNc∑h,ℏ∫dxd2k16π3⁢Ψh,h¯*γ(x,k-x¯q)Ψh,h¯π(x,k)δh,-h¯,(A10)where we have used the fact that [48] v¯h¯(1-x,-k)x(1-x)γ+uh(x,k)x=2P+δh,-h¯.(A11)Fourier transforming to b-space, we obtain ⟨γ(P′)|JEM+|π0(P)⟩=2P+efNc4π∫dxd2be-ix¯q·b⁢∑h,h¯Ψh,h¯*γ(x,b)Ψh,h¯π(x,b)δh,-h¯,(A12)where the real photon wave function, derived using perturbative QED, is given by [49] Ψh,ℏγ(x,b)=-2ef{ieiφ(xδh+,h¯--(1-x)δh-,h¯+)mqK1(mqb⊥)2π+δh+,h¯+K0(mqb⊥)2π}.(A13)Note that Eq. (A13) differs from the photon wave function given in [49] by an overall factor of Nc/(4π) on the right-hand side. This is because we have already extracted the overall color factor in Eq. (A7) and we have implicitly multiplied the photon wave function by 4π to account for the normalization-mismatch mentioned above. The pion wave function is given by Ψh,ℏπ(x,b)=κπX(x)exp(-κ2x(1-x)b⊥22)12hδh,-ℏ,(A14)i.e. the product of Eq. (17) with the pion’s helicity wave function.4
We assume that this helicity wave function is momentum independent. For momentum-dependent helicity wave functions, see [50–52].

(A12), summing over all helicities, and performing the angular integration, we find ⟨γ(P′)|JEM+|π0(P)⟩=P+ef2κNcπ∫dxX(x)⁢∫db⊥mqb⊥K1(mqb⊥)×exp(-κ2x(1-x)b⊥22)⁢J1(b⊥(1-x)Q).(A15)Since the flavor wave function of the neutral pion is |π0⟩=12|uu¯-dd¯⟩, we must take ef2=12(eu2-ed2)=132. (A6), we find Q2Fπγ(Q2)=2κQ3π∫01dxX(x)∫0∞db⊥(mqb⊥)K1(mqb⊥)×exp(-κ2x(1-x)b⊥22)J1(b⊥(1-x)Q),(A16)which is Eq. (22) given that X(x)=x(1-x)χ(x).

app.label: APPENDIX B:
app.title: CHIRAL LIMIT BEHAVIOR
app.p:
In the chiral limit, models A, B and C predict that χ(0)(x)=1, χ(0)(x)=6x(1-x) and χ(0)(x)=30x(1-x) respectively.5
The superscript indicates we take the massless quark limit. Model A thus predicts that X(0)(x)=x(1-x) which is often referred to as the longitudinal mode of light-front holography. More precisely, X(x)=x(1-x) results from the holographic mapping of the pion electromagnetic or gravitational form factor in physical spacetime and AdS5 with a hard-wall geometry [26–28] which is different from the AdS5 soft-wall geometry that generates Eq. (15).

We now investigate the extent to which the chiral limit of our models satisfy two important results: the Brodsky-Lepage (BL) limit and the ABJ chiral anomaly relation. The first result concerns the celebrated Brodsky-Lepage formula for the transition form factor [48], Q2Fπγ(Q2)=2fπ3∫dx(1-x)φπ(x,(1-x)Q)+O(αs,mq2Q2),(B1)where φπ(x,(1-x)Q) is the pion distribution amplitude (DA). Taking the Q2→∞ and mq→0 limit, Eq. (B1) becomes limQ2→∞Q2Fπγ(0)(Q2)=2fπ(0)3∫dx(1-x)φπ(x,∞),(B2)where φπ(x,∞) is the asymptotic DA given by φπ(x,∞)=6x(1-x),(B3)as obtained in conformal QCD [53]. Substituting Eq. (B3) in Eq. (B2) results in limQ2→∞Q2Fπγ(0)(Q2)2fπ(0)=1,(B4)which is the BL limit. The second result is the ABJ relation, Eq. (33), which we rewrite as 22π2Fπγ(0)(0)fπ(0)=1(B5)to emphasize that the ABJ relation is derived in the chiral limit.6
A pedagogical derivation of Eq. (B5) can be found in [54].

We now proceed to find the chiral limits of Eqs. (20) and (22), the latter both in the Q2→∞ and Q2→0 limits. The chiral limit of Eq. (20) is fπ(0)=6πκ∫dxx(1-x)χ(0)(x).(B6)To find the chiral limit of Eq. (A16), note that when mq→0, (mqb⊥)K1(mqb⊥)→1, since the Gaussian in Eq. (A16) exponentially suppresses large b⊥ for any reasonable χ(0)(x). The b⊥ integral in Eq. (22) can then be performed, yielding Q2Fπγ(0)(Q2)=2κ3π∫dxx(1-x)χ(0)(x)⁢(1-exp(-(1-x)Q22κ2x))1(1-x).(B7)If Q2→∞, Eq. (B7) becomes limQ2→∞Q2Fπγ(0)(Q2)=2κ3π∫dxx(1-x)χ(0)(x).(B8)On the other hand, taking the Q2→0 limit of Eq. (B7) we obtain Fπγ(0)(0)=13πκ∫dx(1-x)xχ(0)(x).(B9)Notice that any model with n<0 leads to end point divergences.

Table III indicates the extent to which models A–C accord with ABJ and BL predictions. The BL limit is satisfied exactly for model B and approximately for models A and C. On the other hand, none of the models satisfy the ABJ relation. Model B overestimates the ABJ prediction by exactly a factor of 2. This result was reported previously in [46,55]. In fact, Eq. (B7) with model B for χ(0)(x) coincides with holographic TFF derived in [46].7
More precisely, [46] replaces the right-hand side of Eq. (3) by Pqq¯. If we take Pqq¯=1, then the holographic TFF of [46] coincides exactly with Eq. (B7) [with χ(0)(x) given by model B] and also with the TFF derived in [55]. This should all be set in the context of the fact that our results with mq≠0 do agree with the ABJ relation.
